title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression
\[\begin{align}
\hat{Y} &= b_0 + \beta_1 X
\end{align}\]
\[\large \hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + \dots+b_kX_k\]

Simple as adding predictors to our linear equation



Simple regression on top, multiple regression below
We just keep adding terms
Q: what do you anctipate to change in the outputs?

– A: Each X gets its own slope

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
\[\large \hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + \dots+b_kX_k\]

\(\hat{Y}\) = predicted value on the outcome variable Y
\(b_0\) = predicted value on Y when all Xs = 0
\(X_k\) = predictor variables
\(b_k\) = unstandardized regression coefficients
\(k\) = the number of predictor variables



Let’s break this apart
Y-hat is our prediction
b₀ is the intercept — Y when all predictors are zero (just like SLR)
Each b is a slope, each X is a predictor
k is how many predictors we have

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Straight Line to Hyperplane



More than two predictors (plane)

Multi-dimensional space

Regression coefficients are “partial” regression coefficients

Slope for variable X1 (\(b_1\)) predicts the change in Y per unit X1 holding X2 constant
Slope for variable X2 (\(b_2\)) predicts the change in Y per unit X2 holding X1 constant













With one predictor we had a line that was fit to the data
With Two predictors we are fitting a plane
More than two: terminology is a hyperplane (hard to visualize)
Key insight: each coefficient is now “partial” – It tells you the effect of X₁ after controlling for X₂ – what does that mean? It means, you stay at a fixed point in X1, then X2 has a slope – 2 different slopes => 2 coefficients

Individual Predictors

We test the individual predictors with a t-test:

\(t = \frac{b}{SE}\)
Therefore, the model for each individual predictor is our coefficient b
Single sample t-test to determine if the b value is different from zero




How do we test if each predictor matters?
Same t-test logic
Take the coefficient, divide by its standard error
(Many of these tests are SNR / proportion of variance explained)
Is b different from zero? That’s our question for each predictor

title: Multiple Regression
text:
More predictors => more problems

Assumptions

Linearity
Independence
Normality of residuals
Equal error (“homoskedasticity”)



Issues:

Missingness
Factors are correlated with one another (multicollinearity)
Unusual values/outliers




More predictors = more things can go wrong
Standard assumptions still apply: linearity, independence, normality, homoskedasticity
New issues: missing data, multicollinearity, outliers
Let’s tackle each

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Problems

Missingness

list-wise deletion (removes entire row where missingness occurs)



nomiss <- master %>%
  drop_na() # drop missing data

#base r
nomiss <- master %>%
  na.omit() 

nrow(master)

[1] 267

nrow(nomiss)

[1] 266




Missing data? R uses listwise deletion by default
One missing value in a row? Whole row gone
We went from 267 to 266 — not bad here
Can be catastrophic with more missingness
Later in the semester, we’ll look at other solutions

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Problems

Multicolinearity

You want X and Y to be correlated
You do not want the Xs to be highly correlated





We want X and Y correlated
We don’t want the Xs correlated with each other
Figure: We want as much of the red circle to be calculated!
Next: we also want blues to be seperated! If predictors overlap too much, we can’t untangle their unique effects!! which variable to give credit to! It’s also redundancy.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Problems

Extreme cases (complete collinearity) = Nonidentifiable model
“Unstable” regression coefficients (“bouncing betas”)

Imprecise estimation

Large standard errors

Increased Type II errors

Not detecting a difference when there is one






Extreme case: predictors perfectly correlated — model can’t be estimated at all
Less extreme: “bouncing betas” — coefficients become unstable
Standard errors inflate
You miss real effects (Type II errors)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Tolerance

Measures influence of one predictor on another
If predictors are highly correlated, tolerance gets smaller


\[Tolerance=1- R^2_j\]

where \(R^2_j\) is the proportion of variation in X that is explained by the linear combination of the other predictors in the model



Tolerance: how much variance in X₁ is NOT explained by other Xs
Formula: 1 - R²
Lower tolerance = more problematic
The predictor is redundant with others
“How much unique information do I have about X1?”

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

VIF (variance inflation factor)

How much does our estimates (SEs) change due to the correlation


\[VIF=\frac{1}{1- R^2_j}\]

Rule of thumb:

VIF > 10 indicates issues




VIF is the inverse of tolerance
“How much damage is being done?”
How much are standard errors inflated due to collinearity?
Rule of thumb: VIF > 10 is trouble, some say > 5

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Check multicolinearity in your data


#easystats performance package
#plot(check_collinearity(model_fit))



Easy to check with check_collinearity()
Our predictors look fine — low VIF values
No multicollinearity concerns here

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Strategies

Anticipate collinearity issues at the design stage
Depends: Drop variable if there’s no theoretical pay-off anyway
Depends: Fit separate models and compare fit
Depends: Increase sample size
Depends: Orthogonalize predictors experimentally
Depends: Use alternative approaches, such as ridge regression or LASSO
Do not do anything about it (if prediction is your goal)




What if you have multicollinearity?
Options depend on your goal
Drop redundant predictors, combine them into composites
Use regularization (ridge, LASSO)
Increase sample size
Or — if predicting is all you care about — ignore it
Predictions stay fine; it’s the individual coefficients that suffer

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Identifying unusual cases



Outliers matter more in regression
One weird point can drag the whole line
We need systematic ways to find them

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Influential points

An observation or case is influential if removing it substantially changes the coefficients of the regression model


Influence = Leverage x Distance (outliers)




Key formula: Influence = Leverage × Distance
Leverage: how extreme is the X value?
Distance: how far is Y from the prediction?
Both matter — high leverage + large residual = influential point

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Influential points

Influential points have a large impact on the coefficients and standard errors used for inference

Can be on x or y variables

These points can sometimes be identified in a scatterplot if there is only one predictor variable

This is often not the case when there are multiple predictors

We will use measures to quantify an individual observation’s influence on the regression model

Leverage, Standardized residuals , and Cook’s distance




These points mess with your coefficients and standard errors
With one predictor, you might spot them in a scatterplot
Multiple predictors? Need diagnostic measures
Three key measures: leverage, standardized residuals, Cook’s distance

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage

Deals with Xs


Measure of geometric distance of the observation’s predictor point (\(X_{i1}\), \(X_{i2}\)) from center point of the predictor space

\[
h_i = \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\left(x_i -\overline{x}\right)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}{\left(x_j -\overline{x}\right)^2}} \qquad \text{and}\qquad \overline{h} = \dfrac{k}{n}  \qquad \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{1}{n} \leq h_i \leq 1.0
\]






Note


In multiple regression \(h_i\) measures distance from the centroid (point of means) of Xs





Leverage (h): how unusual is this observation’s X values?
Far from the center of predictor space = high leverage
Points on the edge of the X distribution have more “pull” on the regression line

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage



Visual representation
Points far from the center have high leverage
They have more influence on where the line goes
Not necessarily bad — but watch them

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage

We say a point is high leverage if:

\[
h_i > \frac{2K+2}{N}
\]

K is the number of predictors
N is the sample size


k <- 3 ##number of IVs/predictors
# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*+2)/nrow(.),1, 0))

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Standardized Residuals

Distance

how far away y point is from line


\[
std.res_i = \frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon\sqrt{1-h_i}}
\]

Where \(\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon\) is regression standard error


Use cut-off > 3



Now the Y side
How far is each point from the line?
Standardized residuals account for leverage too
Rule: |standardized residual| > 3 is suspicious

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Standardized Residuals

# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0), 
         std_out=ifelse(abs(.std.resid) > 3, 1, 0))


library(olsrr)

ols_plot_resid_stand(model_fit)




Visual inspection
Most residuals cluster near zero
Outliers stick out
The olsrr package makes nice plots

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and Distance

Montoya

Four quadrants to think about
Low leverage + small residual: typical points (good)
This is what we want most of our data to look like

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and distance

Montoya

High leverage + small residual: unusual X but fits the pattern
Low leverage + large residual: unusual Y but not very influential
These are less concerning

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and distance

Montoya

High leverage + large residual: TROUBLE
These are your influential points
They can dramatically change your regression line

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Cook’s distance

Influence (Cook’s Distance)

A measure of how much of an effect that single case has on the whole model

How close it lies to general line (residuals)
It’s leverage \[
D_i = \frac{(std.res_i)^2}{k + 1}\bigg(\frac{h_i}{1-h_i}\bigg)
\]
Threshold:



\[
\frac{4}{N-K-1}
\]


Cook’s D combines everything
How much would coefficients change if we removed this point?
Formula incorporates both leverage and residuals
Threshold: 4/(n-k-1)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Cook’s distance

# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0),
         std_out=ifelse(abs(.std.resid) > 3, 1, 0), 
         cook_out = ifelse(.cooksd > (4 / (nrow(.) - 3 - 1)), 1, 0))


library(olsrr)
ols_plot_cooksd_bar(model_fit)




Bar plot of Cook’s D
Tall bars = influential points
Easy to spot
Red line is threshold

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Combine Metrics

What do I do with all these numbers?

Create a total score for the number of indicators a data point has
You can decide what rule to use, but a suggestion is 2 or more indicators is an outliers



# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0), cook_out = ifelse(.cooksd > (4 / (nrow(.) - 3 - 1)), 1, 0), std_out=ifelse(.std.resid >= 3, 1, 0)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(sum_out=lev_out+cook_out+std_out) %>%
  filter(sum_out < 2)


nrow(nomiss)

[1] 266

nrow(model_out)

[1] 255




Multiple indicators, multiple decisions
My suggestion: flag points that exceed 2+ thresholds
More robust than any single measure
Create a sum score, filter out the problems

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Easystats: Check_outliers

Use consensus method

If half of methods say point is outlier, get rid of it



# will estimate all outliers methods
outliers_list <- check_outliers(model_fit, method = "all")

# provides a col called outliers with prob of outliers by method (50% more than half said ob was outlier)

out_data <-insight::get_data(model_fit)[outliers_list, ] # Show outliers data

# get rid of values in outliers list in the main dataset 
clean_data <- anti_join(nomiss,out_data, by=c("CESD_total", "PIL_total", "AUDIT_TOTAL_NEW", "DAST_TOTAL_NEW"))



Even easier: check_outliers() with method = “all”
Uses multiple methods
Consensus approach: if half the methods flag it, remove it
Clean and principled

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Refit model

model_fit <- lm(CESD_total ~ PIL_total + AUDIT_TOTAL_NEW + DAST_TOTAL_NEW,
             data = clean_data) 



After removing outliers, refit
Now we have clean data
Our inferences will be more trustworthy

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

Linearity
Independence
Normality of residuals
Equal error (“homoskedasticity”)



Additivity (more than one variable)



Back to basics
Linearity, independence, normality, homoskedasticity
Plus one new one for multiple regression: additivity
Effects of predictors shouldn’t depend on each other — unless you model interactions

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

Additivity

Implies that for an existing model, the effect of a predictor on a response variable (whether it be linear or non-linear) is not affected by changes in other existing predictors

Add interaction if not the case





Additivity means: effect of X₁ doesn’t change across levels of X₂
If it does, you need an interaction term
We’ll cover interactions later

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

performance::check_model(model_fit, check=c("normality", "linearity", "homogeneity", "qq", "vif"))

We can use robust SEs
They work by changing the covariance matrix (the diagonal is the variance)
\[
\text{Var}(\epsilon) = \sigma^2 I_n = \sigma^2
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]



check_heteroscedasticity() detected a problem (p = .001)
Variance isn’t constant — our standard errors are wrong

They adjust the covariance matrix

Step 1

Transform probability into odds

The “odds” of an event are just the probability it happens divided by the probability it does not happen



\[\textrm{Odds} = \frac{\# \textrm{successes}}{\# \textrm{failures}}=
\frac{\# \textrm{successes}/n}{\# \textrm{failures}/n}=

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Logit Link



Step 2

When we convert a probability to odds, odds always > 0

Asymmetric
Curvy

Problematic for linear model


Solution: take log of the odds

\[logit = log(\frac{p}{1-p})\]














If you look at the figure here, we have the odds scale..
P as a function of odds –> bounded to 0. P<0.5 is crammed to this region, and the rest extends to infinity

Odds are always positive and asymmetric — an odds of 2 means twice as likely but an odds of 0.5 means half as likely.
Now we can take the log


Suddenly — symmetric. Zero sits in the middle. p < 0.5 goes negative. p > 0.5 goes positive. Equal room on both sides.
This is a scale where regression works!

section: Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]
text:
Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]


Logit link (today)

Maps probability \((0, 1)\) → log-odds \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\]

Used for: Binomial / Logistic models
Inverse (logistic function) produces the S-curve
Effect on outcome: compressed near 0 and 1


Log link (coming soon)

Maps positive values \((0, +\infty)\) → real line \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]

Used for: Poisson / Count models
Inverse is exponentiation: \(\mu = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}\)
Effect on outcome: exponential scaling









Note


Both links solve the same problem — mapping a constrained parameter onto an unconstrained linear model. The logit handles probabilities; the log handles positive counts.

Step 1

Transform probability into odds

The “odds” of an event are just the probability it happens divided by the probability it does not happen

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)

Logit Link



Step 2

When we convert a probability to odds, odds always > 0

Asymmetric
Curvy

Problematic for linear model


Solution: take log of the odds

\[logit = log(\frac{p}{1-p})\]














If you look at the figure here, we have the odds scale..
P as a function of odds –> bounded to 0. P<0.5 is crammed to this region, and the rest extends to infinity

Odds are always positive and asymmetric — an odds of 2 means twice as likely but an odds of 0.5 means half as likely.
Now we can take the log


Suddenly — symmetric. Zero sits in the middle. p < 0.5 goes negative. p > 0.5 goes positive. Equal room on both sides.
This is a scale where regression works!

text:
Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]


Logit link (today)

Maps probability \((0, 1)\) → log-odds \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\]

Used for: Binomial / Logistic models
Inverse (logistic function) produces the S-curve
Effect on outcome: compressed near 0 and 1


Log link (coming soon)

Maps positive values \((0, +\infty)\) → real line \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]

Used for: Poisson / Count models
Inverse is exponentiation: \(\mu = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}\)
Effect on outcome: exponential scaling









Note


Both links solve the same problem — mapping a constrained parameter onto an unconstrained linear model. The logit handles probabilities; the log handles positive counts.

Simulation with a Data Generating Process
8 coins. 20 tosses each.
Each coin has a small lead weight on the heads side. More lead => higher probability of heads.

# --- DATA GENERATING FUNCTION ---
# Lead weight (grams) determines each coin's bias
coins <- tibble(
  coin        = 1:8,
  lead_weight = 1:8,
  true_p      = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 0.95)
)

# Flip each coin 20 times (individual tosses)
individual <- coins %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(outcomes = list(rbinom(20, 1, true_p))) %>%
  unnest(outcomes) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(coin) %>%
  mutate(toss = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup()

# Aggregate to counts (same data, summarized)
tosses <- individual %>%
  group_by(coin, lead_weight, true_p) %>%
  summarize(
    heads      = sum(outcomes),
    tails      = 20 - heads,
    observed_p = heads / 20,
    .groups    = "drop"
  )

Option 2: Let the model handle it
glm() doesn’t transform your data. It works from the other direction.


Propose a line in log-odds: \(\;\text{logit}(\hat{p}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)




Convert to predicted probabilities: \(\;\hat{p} = \text{plogis}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)\)

text:
Option 2: The model’s predictions gets a new scale
The model’s predicted probability \(\hat{p}\) can be expressed \(\hat{p}\) on three scales:


Probability

Bounded: \([0, 1]\)
S-shaped
What you want to estimate and interpret
Can’t use OLS


Odds

Bounded: \([0, +\infty)\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\)
Still undesirable for OLS


Log-odds

Unbounded: \((-\infty, +\infty)\)
\(\log\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\)
Model is happy because now there’s a Linear relationship
And you’re happy because you can map it to an interpetable parameter

What is Maximum Likelihood?
In OLS — we minimize the squared residuals. Closed-form solution.
With binary data — squared residuals don’t make sense. Instead:

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
Find the parameter values that make the observed data least surprising/ most likely.


The logic:

Propose some parameter values (\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\))
Ask: if these were the true values, how probable is the data I actually got?
Score that probability — the likelihood
Repeat with different values until the likelihood is as high as possible



The parameters at the peak = the maximum likelihood estimates.


MLE for logistic regression
How does MLE apply to our problem?

The model proposes a straight line in log-odds: \(\;\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{lead_weight}\)


Converts to probabilities: \(\;\hat{p}_i = \text{plogis}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)\) for each observation


Scores against the data:

Observation got a 1 ●? Score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
Observation got a 0 ●? Score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better



Total likelihood = multiply all the scores: \(\;\;L = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \hat{p}_i^{y_i}(1-\hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\)


Try thousands of lines → find the one with the highest \(L\).
That line’s \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are your estimates.


MLE: Example with candidates
Three candidate lines — which one fits our coin data best?


Where does the score come from?
Model predicts \(\hat{p} = 0.88\) for the 6g coin. It lands heads. How likely was that?

*Bernoulli Likelihood formula:**
\[L(\hat{p}_i) = \hat{p}_i^{\,y_i} \cdot (1 - \hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\]
\(y = 1\): just \(\hat{p}\). \(\;\;\) \(y = 0\): just \(1 - \hat{p}\).


Two observations? Multiply. 160 observations? Multiply all scores → likelihood.
But 160 tiny numbers multiplied → computer underflow. So we take the log:
\[\log {L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log(\hat{p}_i) + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \hat{p}_i) \right]\]
Same ranking and same peak (what we need for max). And numerically stable.

Build the likelihood from a single observation. Left panel: if the coin lands heads (Y=1), the likelihood IS the predicted probability. The grey line is L(p̂) = p̂ — a straight line. At p̂ = 0.88, the green dot reads off 0.88. High prediction for an event that happened → high score. Right panel: same prediction, but tails (Y=0). Now L(p̂) = 1 − p̂. At p̂ = 0.88, the red dot reads off 0.12. The model predicted 88% heads but got tails — low score, the model was surprised.
The formula combines both. When y=1, the exponents collapse to p̂. When y=0, they collapse to 1−p̂.
For multiple observations, multiply. But 160 numbers between 0 and 1 multiplied together → astronomically small. Like 10⁻⁴⁷. Computers can’t handle that — underflow. So we take the log. Log turns products into sums. Same ranking — if likelihood A beats likelihood B, log-likelihood A also beats log-likelihood B. Same peak. Just stable arithmetic. (J: Let me show you exactly where the score comes from. Left panel — the coin lands heads. The likelihood function for a single heads is just a straight line: the higher your predicted probability, the higher your score. Our model predicted 0.88, so the score is 0.88. Green dot, right there. Right panel — same prediction, but tails happened. Now the likelihood goes the other way — high prediction for something that didn’t happen means a LOW score. 0.12. The model was wrong and the score shows it. The formula at the bottom just wraps both cases into one expression. Now — multiply 160 of these scores together and you get the likelihood. Problem is, 160 numbers less than 1 multiplied together gives you something tiny — like 10 to the negative 47. Computers can’t handle that. So we take the log. Addition instead of multiplication. Same answer, same winner, just numbers your computer can actually store.)



Scoring each guess
For each observation:

If \(Y_i = 1\) (heads ●): score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
If \(Y_i = 0\) (tails ●): score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better

Log-likelihood = sum of log(scores) across all observations

compute_ll <- function(b0, b1, data) {
  p_hat <- plogis(b0 + b1 * data$lead_weight)
  sum(data$outcomes * log(p_hat) + (1 - data$outcomes) * log(1 - p_hat))
}

Interpreting log-odds coefficients as if they were probabilities

text:
What is Maximum Likelihood?
In OLS — we minimize the squared residuals. Closed-form solution.
With binary data — squared residuals don’t make sense. Instead:

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
Find the parameter values that make the observed data least surprising/ most likely.


The logic:

Propose some parameter values (\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\))
Ask: if these were the true values, how probable is the data I actually got?
Score that probability — the likelihood
Repeat with different values until the likelihood is as high as possible



The parameters at the peak = the maximum likelihood estimates.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
MLE for logistic regression
How does MLE apply to our problem?

The model proposes a straight line in log-odds: \(\;\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{lead_weight}\)


Converts to probabilities: \(\;\hat{p}_i = \text{plogis}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)\) for each observation


Scores against the data:

Observation got a 1 ●? Score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
Observation got a 0 ●? Score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better



Total likelihood = multiply all the scores: \(\;\;L = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \hat{p}_i^{y_i}(1-\hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\)


Try thousands of lines → find the one with the highest \(L\).
That line’s \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are your estimates.

section: Where does the score come from?
text:
Where does the score come from?
Model predicts \(\hat{p} = 0.88\) for the 6g coin. It lands heads. How likely was that?

*Bernoulli Likelihood formula:**
\[L(\hat{p}_i) = \hat{p}_i^{\,y_i} \cdot (1 - \hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\]
\(y = 1\): just \(\hat{p}\). \(\;\;\) \(y = 0\): just \(1 - \hat{p}\).


Two observations? Multiply. 160 observations? Multiply all scores → likelihood.
But 160 tiny numbers multiplied → computer underflow. So we take the log:
\[\log {L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log(\hat{p}_i) + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \hat{p}_i) \right]\]
Same ranking and same peak (what we need for max). And numerically stable.

Build the likelihood from a single observation. Left panel: if the coin lands heads (Y=1), the likelihood IS the predicted probability. The grey line is L(p̂) = p̂ — a straight line. At p̂ = 0.88, the green dot reads off 0.88. High prediction for an event that happened → high score. Right panel: same prediction, but tails (Y=0). Now L(p̂) = 1 − p̂. At p̂ = 0.88, the red dot reads off 0.12. The model predicted 88% heads but got tails — low score, the model was surprised.
The formula combines both. When y=1, the exponents collapse to p̂. When y=0, they collapse to 1−p̂.
For multiple observations, multiply. But 160 numbers between 0 and 1 multiplied together → astronomically small. Like 10⁻⁴⁷. Computers can’t handle that — underflow. So we take the log. Log turns products into sums. Same ranking — if likelihood A beats likelihood B, log-likelihood A also beats log-likelihood B. Same peak. Just stable arithmetic. (J: Let me show you exactly where the score comes from. Left panel — the coin lands heads. The likelihood function for a single heads is just a straight line: the higher your predicted probability, the higher your score. Our model predicted 0.88, so the score is 0.88. Green dot, right there. Right panel — same prediction, but tails happened. Now the likelihood goes the other way — high prediction for something that didn’t happen means a LOW score. 0.12. The model was wrong and the score shows it. The formula at the bottom just wraps both cases into one expression. Now — multiply 160 of these scores together and you get the likelihood. Problem is, 160 numbers less than 1 multiplied together gives you something tiny — like 10 to the negative 47. Computers can’t handle that. So we take the log. Addition instead of multiplication. Same answer, same winner, just numbers your computer can actually store.)

Scoring each guess
For each observation:

If \(Y_i = 1\) (heads ●): score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
If \(Y_i = 0\) (tails ●): score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better

Log-likelihood = sum of log(scores) across all observations

compute_ll <- function(b0, b1, data) {
  p_hat <- plogis(b0 + b1 * data$lead_weight)
  sum(data$outcomes * log(p_hat) + (1 - data$outcomes) * log(1 - p_hat))
}

text:
Reporting






Tip


We fitted a logistic model with a logit link (estimated using ML) with sex and bmipct predicting desire to lose weight (formula: lose.wt.01 ~ 1 + female+ bmipct). The model’s explanatory power is substantial (Tjur’s \(R^2\) =0.30). The probability of females wanting to lose weight was 33% higher, b= 1.86, 95% CI [1.37, 2.38], p < .001; OR = 2.98, 95% CI [3.93, 10.9]. An increase in BMI was associated with an increased probability of wanting to lose weight, b = 0.05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.06], p < .001, OR = 1.05, 95% CI [1.04, 1.06]. Looking at the average marginal effect, 1 unit increases in BMI was associated with a 80% increase in desire to lose weight.

Reporting Checklist

Report the link function and estimation method (e.g., logit link, ML estimation)
Report log-odds coefficients and odds ratios with 95% CIs
Report a measure of model fit (McFadden \(R^2\), Tjur \(R^2\), etc.)
Consider reporting marginal effects for practical significance
Include sample size, number of events, and events-per-variable ratio
Mention any convergence issues or model diagnostics

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Common Mistakes

Interpreting log-odds coefficients as if they were probabilities
Forgetting that effects are non-linear on the probability scale

A 1-unit change in X does not have a constant effect on P(Y=1)

Using \(R^2\) from linear regression — use pseudo \(R^2\) measures instead
Not checking for multicollinearity (VIF still applies!)
